 Preview: KU to begin Players Era 8 with UNLV matchup
 By Henry Greenstein     Nov 16, 2026
 AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh 
 Kansas head coach Bill Self, center right, and guard Taylen Kinney (0) watch during the first half of an NCAA college basketball game against Kentucky in State Farm Champions Classic in Chicago, Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. 
 The Kansas men’s basketball team accomplished what precious few do last season by going home from Las Vegas richer than it arrived.
 The Jayhawks won all three of their games at the Players Era tournament and took home $300,000 in prize money via name, image and likeness opportunities as the event’s third-place team (they wound up in the third-place match against Tennessee, which they won in dramatic fashion, due to point differential).
 This year, KU will return as part of the newly expanded tournament’s Players Era 8, which features a more straightforward bracket format and gives the Jayhawks three guaranteed games during the week before Thanksgiving.
 Head coach Bill Self told reporters he prefers this format to the Players Era 16, which takes place the following week, because the possibility of having to play a fourth game — which only the top two teams get to do — prevents teams in the 16-team group from being certain that they can schedule up to the single-season total of 32 games and maximize revenue from home contests.
 KU, for its part, is assured of three games in three days, and that gantlet begins on Tuesday night at 8:30 p.m. Central Time against UNLV. Depending on results, the Jayhawks could face Auburn or West Virginia on Wednesday and then Florida, Houston, Notre Dame or Rutgers after that on Thursday.
 While the Jayhawks don’t begin with one of the strongest teams in the field, before they can get to the high-caliber competition of the Players Era’s second and third rounds, they must play what is essentially a road matchup against a school that plays its own home games just a few miles from Michelob Ultra Arena.
 “It’s a great tournament, but first game we got UNLV,” freshman guard Taylen Kinney told reporters on Friday. “That’s basically a home game for them, so you know they’re going to give us their all first game, so we just got to get through them first.”
 The Rebels are off to a solid 3-0 start, having most recently defeated Stanford 76-68 on Friday night behind a balanced scoring effort of 17 points from Florida State transfer guard Cam Miles, 16 from sophomore forward Tyrin Jones and 15 from a familiar face, Missouri transfer guard Sebastian Mack.
 Mack, who started his career at UCLA, leads UNLV with 21 points per game to this point in the year, in large part because he went off for 31 in the Rebels’ season opener against Northern Arizona. Two additional transfers, guard Dontrez Williams (Lindenwood) and center Jeremy Foumena (UCF), fill out UNLV’s starting lineup.
 Perhaps the Rebels’ most impressive accomplishment of the year so far came in a game that didn’t count, when they outscored Mack’s former team Missouri by 14 in a second half to beat the Tigers 90-81 in exhibition action. Miles finished one rebound shy of a triple-double in that unofficial contest.
 “They’re fast, they’re athletic and they’re going to try to take you out of what you want to try to do,” Self said.
 Self also noted that UNLV has as good of a young prospect as there’ll be in Vegas. That could be a reference to Jackson Kiss, a 6-foot-8 forward who is the Mountain West’s preseason freshman of the year and was once committed to Iowa State. Kiss, originally from New Zealand, is averaging 6.3 points and 3.7 rebounds off the bench to this point.
 UNLV head coach Josh Pastner, formerly of Memphis and Georgia Tech, will be looking for a big win to launch his second season leading the Rebels.
 “Every game this early in the season puts you in different situations,” Self said. “Vegas is going to switch defenses a lot, and Josh is going to do some different things that we haven’t seen yet, so how do you adjust on the fly as opposed to coming down and backing it out and getting organized, which I hate playing that way.”
 KU will hope to build on the momentum from last week’s Champions Classic victory over Kentucky, one that earned it national plaudits and demonstrated that it can play with pace and ball movement even without injured point guard Melvin Council Jr.
 The Jayhawks will have to draw on their depth throughout the Players Era: “In three games in three days, obviously deeper teams would have an advantage,” Self said, “and can we actually take advantage of people that way?”
 NO. 11 KANSAS JAYHAWKS (3-0) VS. UNLV REBELS (3-0) 
 • Michelob Ultra Arena, Las Vegas, 8:30 p.m. Central time
 • Broadcast: ESPN
 • Radio: Jayhawk Radio Network (in Lawrence, KLWN AM 1320 / K269GB FM 101.7 / KKSW FM 105.9 / KMXN FM 92.9)
 KEEP AN EYE OUT 
 Out of stock: At one point this offseason, this Players Era opener looked like it was setting up to be an AJ Storr revenge game for the Rebels. The former St. John’s, Wisconsin, KU and Ole Miss wing, who struggled as a junior at KU but returned to form with 15.5 points per game for Ole Miss as a senior, joined UNLV late in the summer when he seemed poised to get a fifth year via the courts. But he hasn’t remained consistently eligible despite a series of legal efforts. However, Storr was part of a lawsuit filed on Friday in Tippecanoe County, Indiana, court (the one that also includes two KU baseball players) and seeks an immediate temporary restraining order; how quickly, if at all, an Indiana judge wants to oblige will determine whether he can take the court at all in the Players Era.
 Finding his way: Self discussed the importance of depth entering the endurance test of the Players Era, but the Jayhawks are still missing one piece on the wing. Sophomore Kohl Rosario took an elbow to the mouth in practice on Oct. 23 that gave him a concussion and required oral surgery. He has missed one exhibition and three regular-season games since and hasn’t yet made his debut for the year. Self told reporters that Rosario has returned to some non-contact work in practice; however, “he’s going to have to pass some more things and go live contact multiple days before we play him, but I think he’s doing better.” If he doesn’t make it against UNLV, he could potentially provide fresh legs for another game later in the Jayhawks’ stay in Las Vegas.
 On the break: Even without the coast-to-coast speed of Council, the Jayhawks showed signs of developing into an elite transition team on both sides of the ball against Kentucky. They tallied a modest 11 fast-break points to the Wildcats’ six, but perhaps even more impressive was their transition defense, as they limited Kentucky to zero points off turnovers. With the speed of players like Kinney and Leroy Blyden Jr. and the athleticism of Tyran Stokes and Keanu Dawes, there’s plenty to like about KU playing with urgency whenever it can; as Self said, “There’s no reason why we shouldn’t get out and run every opportunity, even if it’s not opportunistic, just to play with a faster pace, because I think this team plays better at a fast pace than what it would as a slower pace.”
 OFF-KILTER OBSERVATION 
 Foumena had a key go-ahead bucket for UCF in the second half of the Knights’ 81-75 win over KU at Addition Financial Arena last season.
